default.py:229-237: json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True) emits '<','>','&' only as literal characters inside string values; JSON escape sequences (\n, \", \\, \uXXXX) never contain them, and they are not JSON structural characters. Replacing them with \u003c/\u003e/\u0026 yields valid escapes decoding to the original chars. A literal backslash before '<' is encoded as \\ so result is \\\u003c, which still parses correctly. Elements joined with ',' inside '[' ']' form a valid JSON array.

default.py:222-238: remaining starts as MAX(32768) - len(prefix) - len(suffix) - len(omitted) - 2 (prefix/suffix/omitted are short constants, lines 27-37, so remaining is positive). Each record is added only if cost (len(value) + 1 comma when encoded is non-empty) <= remaining, and remaining is decremented by cost. Output is prefix + '[' + join + ']' + suffix + optional omitted, so its length is prefix+suffix+2+sum(costs)+omitted <= 32768 for all inputs. When no records fit, encoded is empty and the output is prefix+'[]'+suffix+omitted, which stays within budget because omitted is reserved up front whether or not it is appended. Skipped records (continue) do not consume budget, and the comma accounting stays correct because it keys on encoded being non-empty. The test at tests/unit/test_memory_context_boundary.py:78-86 asserts len(out)-len(BASE) <= 32768 with oversized inputs; CHANGELOG.md:82 states the 32,768-character cap.

default.py:204-205 _cap returns value if len<=limit else value[:limit-len(marker)]+marker, so length is exactly limit. Limits: 4000 (line 20), 1000 (line 21), 8000 (line 25); markers lengths 12, 12, 19 (called at 212, 217, 218-219), all far below limits, so slice index is positive.

default.py:229-230: every record is serialized with json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True), then all '<', '>' and '&' are replaced with \u003c, \u003e, \u0026. JSON structure emits no '<' or '>' itself, so none can remain in the output. Hostile input: a stored value containing the literal text \u003c is serialized by json.dumps as \\u003c (the backslash is doubled). The replacements never turn that into a raw '<', and a JSON parser decodes it back to the literal characters, not to a delimiter. Control characters and newlines stay as JSON escapes. Only the fixed prefix and suffix constants (line 237) add delimiters, and they are not memory content. Truncation by _cap happens before escaping, so it cannot split an escape sequence.

default.py:229-230: json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True) escapes newlines/control chars and non-ASCII, quotes and backslashes (so a stored backslash becomes \\ and cannot combine with a following escape); then <, >, & are replaced with \u003c/\u003e/\u0026. Output therefore never contains a raw '<' so '</sqllens_memory_data>' cannot appear in encoded values. Hostile input traced: content '</sqllens_memory_data>' becomes '\u003c/sqllens_memory_data\u003e'; content '\<' becomes '\\\u003c', still no raw '<'. Decoding by a JSON parser yields data, not a delimiter in the raw text.
